newsitem.title: UK: Dollar partially casts off inhibitions post G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar partially casts off inhibitions post G7.

text.p: A lack of overt dollar-quashing comments from the Group of Seven nations at a weekend meeting pushed up the dollar on Monday as bulls cast aside the restraint they had shown before the talks.
G7 finance ministers said on Sunday that major currency misaligments have been corrected and that excessive currency volatility and deviations from fundamentals were undesirable.
The contents of the G7 statement were mostly in line with what the market had expected, with analysts saying the remarks lacked aggressiveness and had made dollar bulls comfortable.
"This is not likely to hold the dollar's rise in the near term, since the tone of the comments was not that strong," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International here.
"Obviously the background is not conducive to halting the dollar's rise given the expectations of fairly strong U.S. data this week and the Fed tightening next month."
However, tha market was prevented from being entirely euphoric because the major nations sounded a warning note on trade imbalances.

They said their meeting emphasised the importance of avoiding currency moves that could lead to a re-emergence of large trade imbalances. No names were named, but markets saw this as a reference to Japan's swelling, politically sensitive trade surplus with the U.S.
Analysts noted that although the dollar had strengthened since the previous G7 meeting in February, the G7's tone had not.
"The market will compare it with the statement in February and they won't see a lot of difference," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy here.
"More importantly, they will see no dissatisfaction with the (dollar's) rise since February. There's nothing in this communique to say this is a bad thing."

The general perception after the G7 meeting appeared to be that G7 authorities would tolerate a strong dollar as long as it did not move rapidly, analysts said, citing a remark made by Bank of England Governor Eddie George after the meeting.
George said G7 officials felt the foreign exchange environment was "in pretty good shape" and that no need had been expressed at the meeting for an action plan to deal with future currency moves.

Relief over the lack of anti-dollar statements drove the dollar to a fresh 37-month high against the mark overnight, while against the yen it rose to within a shade of a 55-month high reached earlier this month.

The dollar was at 1.7330 marks in Europe's mid-morning trade, down from an overnight high of 1.7395 according Bank of Japan data. Against the yen, the dollar was at 126.70, off its overnight high of 127.10. The dollar had been at 1.7246 marks and 125.95 yen in late European trade on Friday before the G7 meeting.

"Providing we don't see the dollar surging above 1.75 (marks) and 130 (yen), the perception is that the authorities are not going to intervene in a coordinated or aggressive fashion," IBJ's Hannah said.

The comment on trade issues did not mean the U.S. would try to drive the yen higher to curb Japan's exports, analysts said. A stronger yen makes Japanese companies less competitive abroad, since it pushes up the prices of their products in terms of foreign currency.

"It appears from (U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin's comments that his he is encouraging efforts to stimulate (Japanese) domestic demand," Paul Chertkow, global head of currency research at UBS here.

"This would be inconsistent with efforts to cap the dollar. Intervention in the past has worked only when accompanied by monetary policy, and with growth in Japan already suffering from tighter fiscal policy, a tightening of monetary policy to cap the dollar would exacerbate the economy," Chertkow said.
